seoDescription: Learn how to set up your complete development environment for C# and .NET in Visual Studio Code with this official beginner guide. This video walks you through the entire process, from installing VS Code and the .NET SDK to configuring the C# Dev Kit extension. You'll see how to create, build, and debug your first application, a web API, in just a few minutes. Discover the powerful features of VS Code for .NET development, including solution management, NuGet integration, testing, and advanced code navigation.

chapters.title: Introduction: Building with C# and .NET
chapters.description: See the wide range of applications you can build with C# and .NET and get an overview of the setup process in VS Code.

chapters.title: Step 1: Install Visual Studio Code
chapters.description: Follow along to download and install Visual Studio Code on your machine, including recommended settings and a look at learning resources.

chapters.title: Step 2: Install the C# Dev Kit
chapters.description: Learn how to find and install the C# Dev Kit extension, which provides comprehensive language support and tooling.

chapters.title: Step 3: Configure the .NET SDK
chapters.description: Walk through the C# Dev Kit setup guide to sign in with a Microsoft account and install the correct .NET SDK version.

chapters.title: Step 4: Create a New .NET Project
chapters.description: Use the VS Code interface to reload the editor, create a new .NET Web API project, and run basic `dotnet` CLI commands.

chapters.title: Navigating Your Project in VS Code
chapters.description: Explore the Solution Explorer for project management, learn how to manage .NET workloads, and see how to add NuGet packages to your application.

chapters.title: Run and Debug Your Web API
chapters.description: Set breakpoints, launch the debugger, step through your C# code, inspect variables, and test the API endpoint.

chapters.title: Next Steps and Further Learning
chapters.description: Discover resources on the .NET website for further learning and see a final summary of the setup process.

summary:
## Core Tools for C# & .NET Development

Your development environment relies on three key components:

*   **Visual Studio Code**: A lightweight, extensible code editor available on Windows, macOS, and Linux.
*   **.NET SDK**: The Software Development Kit that contains the compilers, libraries, and runtimes needed to build and run .NET applications.
*   **C# Dev Kit (VS Code Extension)**: An extension that supercharges VS Code with features for advanced C# development, including project/solution management, a test explorer, and enhanced debugging.

> [!TIP]
> Installing the **C# Dev Kit** will automatically install the base **C#** extension, so you only need to install the Dev Kit to get started.

## Setup Workflow

The recommended setup process is guided by VS Code and the C# Dev Kit:

1.  **Install Visual Studio Code**: Download and run the installer from the official website.
2.  **Install the C# Dev Kit Extension**: Search for `C# Dev Kit` in the VS Code Extensions view and click install.
3.  **Link Your Microsoft Account**: The Dev Kit requires a Visual Studio subscription, including the free Community edition. Sign in when prompted.
4.  **Install the .NET SDK**: The C# Dev Kit's *Getting Started* guide will detect if you are missing the .NET SDK and provide a button to install the latest recommended version automatically.

## Creating and Managing Projects

*   **Create a Project**: Use the Command Palette (`Ctrl+Shift+P` or `Cmd+Shift+P`) and search for **`.NET: New Project`**. This will show a list of available templates (e.g., Web API, Console App, Blazer) and guide you through creating the project in your chosen folder.
*   **Solution Explorer**: The C# Dev Kit adds a **Solution Explorer** view to VS Code, providing a structured `.sln` and `.csproj` based view of your project. This makes managing files, dependencies, and multiple projects easier.
*   **Manage NuGet Packages**: Right-click a project in the Solution Explorer and select **Add NuGet Package...** to search for and install packages from the registry.

## Debugging in VS Code

VS Code provides a first-class debugging experience for C#:

1.  **Set a Breakpoint**: Click in the gutter to the left of a line number to set a breakpoint.
2.  **Start Debugging**: Go to the **Run and Debug** view and click the **Run and Debug** button (or press `F5`).
3.  **Select a Configuration**: Choose the desired launch profile (e.g., HTTP, HTTPS) when prompted.
4.  **Debug**: When your code hits a breakpoint, execution will pause. You can then:
    *   Inspect local variables.
    *   Step over, into, or out of functions.
    *   View the call stack and threads.

## Key CLI Commands

You can run `dotnet` commands directly from the integrated terminal in VS Code:

*   `dotnet --version`: Check the installed SDK version.
*   `dotnet --info`: Display detailed information about your .NET installation.
*   `dotnet workload list`: List all installed workloads (e.g., `maui`, `aspire`).
*   `dotnet workload search`: Search for available workloads to install.

## Further Learning

Once your environment is set up, explore the free resources available at the **.NET website** (`dotnet.microsoft.com`), including:

*   **Beginner Videos** on a wide range of topics.
*   **Tutorials and Courses** for specific application types like web, mobile, and desktop.
*   The **Microsoft Learn C# curriculum**, which is complemented by a freeCodeCamp certification.

## Introduction: Building with C# and .NET

With .NET and C Sharp, you can build anything from AI applications, powerful back ends and front end web applications, mobile, desktop, games, IoT, and so much more. You can do it all in VS Code. I'm going to show you how to set up everything from start to finish in under 10 minutes. Let's go.

## Step 1: Install Visual Studio Code

So, a few places to get started. First would be the .NET website where you can learn all about .NET and everything in there you can build with it. And of course, you can get started and download the SDK.

We're going to start on the Visual Studio Code website. This is going to give me everything I need on VS Code, no matter where I'm developing. Here I can hit the download for Windows or other platforms. And VS Code and .NET are available on Windows, Linux, and Mac. So, I'm going to hit download here. And it's going to start to download VS Code. And what's great here is that it's a nice quick install and gives me everything I need. Now, I'm here on a Windows ARM machine and it's super optimized and downloading the ARM build for me and will install the ARM build of .NET, too. Now, I'm inside of a sandbox, so you probably won't see this, but basically this is going to show that it's going to be a user install of VS Code. So, I'm just going to hit accept here, the default location. And I love the little open with code file extensions. And let's add a desktop icon for good measure and hit install.

Now, as that installs, I also want to point out over here that there's a lot of great documentation, no matter what you're getting started with inside of VS Code. So, here's C Sharp. There's great intro videos and a full getting started doc. Now, this documentation will show you not how to get started with the tools for VS Code, but also the C Sharp curriculum, which is available free on Microsoft Learn.

That also is complementary to the free Code Camp certification for C Sharp. So, you can also do that as well. So, definitely check that out. I'll put links in the show notes, too. All right, VS Code is basically done over here. And let's go ahead and launch it.

## Step 2: Install the C# Dev Kit

So, once VS Code launch, I'm going to go ahead and open it up here a little bit bigger and I'm going to zoom it in here as well. Awesome. So, here I can get started with VS Code. I'm just going to say I did it all perfect.

Now, the first thing we want to do is actually install some extensions. So, I'm going to go ahead and install the C# extension, but we can see the extensions allow me to extend VS Code with different language support and other things to enhance my productivity. So, I'm just going to go up and say C#. And here we're going to see C# and the C# Dev Kit.

C# is sort of the base language support over here to build C# applications inside of VS Code. And the C# Dev Kit gives me a whole bunch of goodies, no matter what I'm developing. So, here I get solution and project management, NuGet integration, testing and environments. I can run and debug my tests and really amazing best-in-class support for code navigation, refactoring, and semantic awareness.

Now, this depends on the C# extension, so it actually gets both of them at the same time. So, you get everything that you need there. So, let's go ahead and let that install really quick.

## Step 3: Configure the .NET SDK

All right, perfect. So, the C# Dev Kit has opened up here and I'm going to get a few different pop-ups. Let's just go ahead and close these for now and let's go through the getting started guide here. Let me just minimize this down and get full screen.

So, the first thing here is that I can link my Microsoft account to use the C# Dev Kit with my Visual Studio subscription, including the free community edition. So, I can click that connect button or here I can click the sign in with Microsoft to use C# Dev Kit. So, I'm going to go ahead and sign in really quick.

All right, so I'm signed in. I'm going to head back over to VS Code and I am good to go and I'm going to go ahead and check that there. Then it's going to say set up environment. So, here if you have the .NET SDK installed already, you can check by opening up the terminal. I don't yet, so that's I'm going to need to install it. So, I could go over to the .NET website and I can click the download button and this is going to give me the download link over here for my version, but of course .NET is available everywhere. So, no matter where you're developing, you can installers and SDKs for Linux, Mac, and Windows. But, VS Code is going to guide it for me automatically by clicking the install.net SDK.

It's going to show me the latest version, so 8.0.301, and I'm just going to go ahead and install it. It's going to download the arm64 version of the .NET SDK and give me everything that I need. So, this takes a minute or so, so let me go ahead and just wait for .NET to finish up.

## Step 4: Create a New .NET Project

All right, perfect. So, the .NET SDK has been installed. Now, I do want to reload VS Code, so I'm just going to go and shut it all down for me. And then I'm just going to go and relaunch it here. And the nice thing is VS Code brings up exactly where I was at. So, I'm just going to minimize these windows, and we are good to go. Now, at this point, this is going to walk me through if I have an existing .NET app, I can open up ASP.NET Core, console apps, libraries. I can create my own project over here. It's going to show me how to launch and debug applications. And there's this learn more. Now, what's really cool is you can open the command palette. And here with the .NET command, you can see all of the different things that you can do. So, I'm just going to mark this as done, and we're totally off to the races.

I'm going to click on the explorer button, and I'm going to say create new .NET project. And a few things are going to happen here when I go out and create this project. It's going to load up all of the templates that are on the .NET SDK. So, you can see ASP.NET Core, APIs, Blazer applications, console apps, Playwright test projects, and a whole lot more. Let's just go ahead and create our very first a web API, which would be great. So, I'm just going to click on that. It's going to ask me where do I want to put the code? So, I'm just going to go ahead and put it into a new folder called code. There we go, that sounds good. Select the folder there. Web application one, perfect, and create the project.

So, this is going to create everything I need. This is just calling the command line. So, for example, here after I trust my author, which is me, I can go into terminal, new terminal, and I can go ahead and start to execute .NET commands.

So, for example, I could go ahead and execute the .NET version command or .NET yeah, version here and this is going to show me 3.0.1. I could do .NET --info and that will show me everything installed on this machine and my .NET SDK.

## Navigating Your Project in VS Code

I can additionally install other workloads. I can do .NET workload list. This is going to show me anything that's available or installed on my machine for .NET workloads such as Aspire or .NET MAUI. So, I could do .NET workload search and this is going to show me additional workloads that I can add on. So, if I want to do MAUI development or Aspire development or just Android or iOS development, I'm good to go there.

So, a few things you want to note over here is you have your traditional file explorer that's part of VS Code. But, if I look down here, I can see a solution explorer and I just love to drag and drop this up top. And now we get all of our different dependencies in this project and solution view. I get my properties going on here. I can right-click on the top here. I can add new projects, add existing projects. I can select the web application and add a NuGet package. If I wanted to search for something like Aspire, for example, it's going to go off and show me all of the Aspire packages that I can install into my app.

## Run and Debug Your Web API

Now, this application here will show me that it's going to go off and create a weather forecast API for me. And from here, I could come into the terminal and I could do .NET run as well, so that'd be great. Or I can start to add some breakpoints into the application, go to the debug window and I'm going to say run in debug and select C#.

And here it's going to ask me what configuration do I want. So I can select the default configuration HTTP or HTTPS. Let's just do the default configuration and let's go ahead and have it build my application and then debug it locally on my machine. So this is really nice because in just a few minutes I have a full application that is ready to go to start building APIs and I'm debugging it as well. So I get all my threads, stack traces and here I get a full swagger. So I can click on the try it out. I can click execute. And this is going to go back over into VS code and I have a breakpoint here. This is going to show me my summary, it's going to show me everything that was generated and I can step through over here and this is going to pick the first five forecasts that are coming in. So I have all this capability which is really really nice.

So that is awesome to see. And here for example I could right click and I can say go to definition and it's going to navigate me in there automatically. So let's go ahead and continue. And if I come back over into the browser and here I can see all the data that's being returned. So that's really really powerful to actually start debugging and do everything that I want right inside of VS code.

## Next Steps and Further Learning

All right, so beyond that if you want to go further now that you have your entire development environment set up, head back over to the .NET website. And on top of learn you can do the learn to code C#. There's amazing beginner videos so you can learn all about building absolutely anything with .NET and one of my favorite areas of course is the tutorial and courses. So if you wanted to get started for example with that back end web, this is going to give you all sorts of different materials that you can get off start building different applications.

Well there you have it, your entire development environment is set up from start to finish with C# .NET and VS code. There's so much more to explore so I'm going to put links in the show notes below to everything that you saw today and so much more. Don't forget if you like this video, jam that like button, share it with a friend, hit that subscribe button as well. So, until next time, thanks for watching.
